title: The gatekeeper
hookLine: mindfulness is like the wise gatekeeper of a frontier fortress (AN 7, the fortress)

cards: At the edge of a kingdom, where the road comes in from foreign land, stands a fortress. Thick walls. A moat.
Soldiers. Storerooms of grain and oil. And at the gate, one person whose whole job is to look at every face that arrives and decide: you, come in; you, I don't know you, wait outside.
Everything inside depends on that one person paying attention. The Buddha drew this fortress in detail, piece by piece.

teach.b: The sutta is in the book of sevens of the Numbered Discourses. A king's frontier fortress, the Buddha says, can't be taken by enemies from outside when it has seven things in place and four kinds of provisions stored.
Then he maps each piece onto a practitioner.
The deep-rooted pillar at the entrance is faith. The moat is a sense of shame about doing wrong. The path patrolled around the walls is fear of wrongdoing.
The weapons are learning, the teachings you've heard. The army is energy. The high, thick rampart is wisdom.
And the gatekeeper, wise, experienced and intelligent, who keeps strangers out and lets known friends in, is mindfulness. He doesn't fight; that's the army's job. He doesn't build the walls.
He knows who's who, and he's at his post.
That's anger, coming up the road. That's kindness, a friend: open the gate.
Without him, the strongest walls are useless; the enemy simply walks in, because no one noticed. A few days ago you guarded the sense doors.

This is the same gate, seen from inside the walls, and it echoes a Dhammapada line from the first year, in Max Müller's words: "Like a well-guarded frontier fort, with defences within and without, so let a man guard himself."
A frontier fort, not a palace: mindfulness stands where ordinary life arrives.

how: Meditation teachers often use the gatekeeper image to describe mindfulness as noticing and naming what arises, and some traditions practice mental noting, labeling each thought or feeling as it appears.

o: a soldier who fights off every bad thought
a wall that keeps every feeling out

games.q: the frontier fortress: tap the pairs.

s: in this simile, mindfulness is the army that fights the enemy
energy is the army; mindfulness is the gatekeeper who recognizes who's arriving.
wisdom is the high rampart of the fortress
the wall is wisdom; the gatekeeper is mindfulness.
he keeps strangers out and lets known friends in.

games.q: you're the gatekeeper. irritation arrives, dressed up as "just being honest." what's your job?
o: recognize him, and keep him outside.
games.why: in the fortress simile the gatekeeper doesn't fight; he knows strangers from friends, keeping out the one and admitting the other.

practice: Picture yourself at the gate as thoughts and moods come up the road, and name each one as it arrives: worry, planning, a memory, irritation, tenderness.
Don't fight any of them; let the friendly ones in, let the strangers wait outside, and stay at your post.

wordCard.voice: The gatekeeper. In the book of sevens, mindfulness is the wise gatekeeper of the frontier fortress, the one who knows who's who.

orig.note: Pali dovārika: gatekeeper, the image for mindfulness in the fortress simile.

carryVoice: Your line: know who's who. The gatekeeper doesn't fight; he recognizes. Three hundred ninety days now.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 7.67 (Nagaropama Sutta, the fortress; 7.63 in some editions)
